Edition note: An independent English rewriting for English-language readers, preserving the Chinese argument while reorganizing context, sequence, and emphasis. Full-series spoilers.

Having sex like a man

In the first episode, Carrie Bradshaw conducts an experiment. She and her friends have been discussing an apparent imbalance in New York's sexual arrangements: men seem able to date, have sex, and leave without emotional obligations, while women are expected to pay something extra. What if a woman simply adopted the same procedure? No attachment, no follow-up questions, no waiting to be dismissed. Carrie decides to try.

She returns to an old lover she has returned to before. They sleep together; afterward, she gets dressed and leaves. Outside, she feels her energy return. She has taken back the initiative, and the exhilaration is real. The experiment works on its own terms. But mastering the procedure cannot answer a different question: is this the life she wants to keep living? The pilot leaves that question open. The next six years begin to answer it.

This opening is often remembered as a provocation announcing an audacious urban sex comedy. It is that, but it also establishes the show's deeper method with unusual precision. Carrie takes a ready-made rule, one that seems to work for other people, and tries fitting herself inside it. She can reproduce every action. What the subsequent story makes visible is the difference between copying an action and becoming the person for whom it makes sense.

A profession made from private lives

Carrie writes a weekly newspaper column about relationships. The arrangement is more than a convenient way to supply voice-over: her own private life and those of her friends provide her livelihood. She dates, and writes. A friend has a crisis, and she writes. Her own heartbreak becomes copy. Six years of approaching and retreating from Big become a succession of questions she can put on a page.

There is an uncomfortable consequence. Experience is not only something she lives; it is something her work continually requires. This is not an accusation that she manufactures trouble. It is a question about the pressure of having a deadline. If you owe your editor another account of your emotional life every week, an uneventful week presents a professional problem. How would she write genuine peace? When another person's ordinary days enter hers, can she remain merely an observer of them?

Her familiar “I couldn't help but wonder” performs a small transformation: something happening becomes something available to be examined. A breakup acquires an angle. A brunch conversation suggests a subject. Pain begins searching for its sentence before it has finished hurting. Such an ability can be a remarkably effective protection. It lets someone stand a little to the side of what she is undergoing.

That protection is also the question the series keeps pressing. How many years can someone spend beside her own life? The column gives Carrie independence, a craft, and a way to survive confusion. It may also give her a way not to be entirely present.

Four women, four directions

The four women begin from different positions. Carrie is the observer, increasingly skilled at explaining what other people want, and not necessarily closer to knowing what she wants herself. Miranda Hobbes, a lawyer working toward partnership, begins with a reasoned and often successful conviction that she does not need anyone. Charlotte York, who works in a gallery, wants a very specific collection of things: a wedding, a suitable husband, a Park Avenue apartment, and children. Samantha Jones runs a public-relations business and does not merely tolerate independence. She enjoys it.

Samantha's position is often a source of jokes, but that does not make the position itself a joke. Nor are the others preliminary stages of enlightenment that she has already completed. Their directions, speeds, and costs differ. What connects their stories is the movement toward becoming more fully themselves.

Carrie's movement is from explaining desire to recognizing her own. Miranda's is from keeping everyone out to discovering that she can let someone in without being overwritten. Charlotte must distinguish the life she wants from the approved package she thought would contain it. Samantha learns that she can love someone deeply without disappearing into the relationship.

“Becoming yourself” can sound like a pleasant slogan. Across six seasons and two films, the series gives it a very concrete bill: marriage, infertility, cancer, a wedding that does not happen, betrayal, miscarriage, and the decision to leave even a good relationship. These are not decorative obstacles on the way to a predetermined happy ending. They are the experiences through which each woman discovers what her choices mean.

Testing the rules

The pilot's borrowed procedure returns in countless other forms. You should marry before thirty-five. Men want one thing and women another. This behavior must conceal that intention. At your age, you cannot afford to be picky. If he wanted to, he would. Carrie collects such formulas as material, tests them, and turns them into questions.

The show is most interesting when it does not refute a formula in an argument. Instead, it places the formula against a particular person and lets the mismatch appear. Charlotte marries in her thirties and finds herself profoundly unhappy. Big approaches and withdraws, with another marriage interrupting their history; one apparently decisive action cannot guarantee a relationship's future. Steve changes, Harry and Charlotte adjust to each other, while Aidan continues to want a life rather different from Carrie's. No single maxim explains them all.

This method has an inconvenient implication. If a rule can fail when it encounters an actual person, there may be no finished set of instructions to follow. Carrie's initial experiment does not fail because sexual freedom is wrong. Samantha often lives happily near precisely that freedom. The same arrangement cannot decide what both women want.

Knowing whether something is yours may require trying it and then asking whether you want to continue. Success at performing the actions is not yet an answer.

The observer's privilege

Narration gives Carrie another kind of power: she can decide what an event means. During her affair with Big, repeated decisions can be organized into a story about being unable to help herself. Each meeting is supposed to be the last. Told from Aidan's side, however, the same events would have a different grammar.

When they reunite in the fourth season, their relationship returns but trust does not simply return with it. Aidan presses for marriage. Carrie finally recognizes that a wedding cannot settle what has already happened. Her account has encountered someone else's experience, and one of the show's achievements is that her ability to make a compelling story does not erase his injury.

Narrating is not synonymous with lying. It can make chaos bearable. Yet it can also carry someone out of an experience before it ends, preparing the version that friends, readers, or a future self will hear. Carrie's column is both an accomplishment and a distance.

The rarer moment is the one in which a person does not hurry to turn experience into a later story. There is no headline yet, no polished question. There is only someone fully there.

Sex and the City, created by Darren Star, aired from 1998 to 2004 across six seasons and ninety-four episodes, followed by films in 2008 and 2010.
